name: Lauren Weeks
who: American Hyrox pioneer and three-time World Champion (2020, 2021, 2023), still ranked world No. 1 in 2026.
why: The most decorated racer in the sport's history and the benchmark every Elite 15 season is measured against.
takeaway: Build a training approach that holds up across years, not just one peak season.

name: Linda Meier
who: Reigning 2025 Hyrox World Champion (58:56), a German IT specialist turned Elite 15 racer.
why: The athlete who just took the world title heading into her title defense in Stockholm.
takeaway: Treat Hyrox as a serious second discipline alongside your day job — a title doesn't require training full-time.

name: Joanna Wietrzyk
who: Australia's fastest Hyrox woman; 2025 World Championship runner-up and multiple major-race winner.
why: A consistent podium threat with a growing sponsor roster including Puma and Amazfit.
takeaway: Chase consistency over one big result — repeat podiums beat a single win.

name: Megan Jacoby
who: 2024 Hyrox World Champion and the first woman ever to break one hour; sat out the 2025 world final.
why: The athlete who broke the sub-hour barrier — her return to a start line is the story to watch.
takeaway: Set one hard time goal, like breaking an hour, and structure training specifically around it.

name: Kris Rugloski
who: 2022 Hyrox World Champion and a 65-race veteran who fought back from a torn meniscus to reclaim her Elite 15 spot at the Barcelona Last Chance Qualifier.
why: A comeback story with real depth — she also races ultras, having debuted at the Barkley Marathons.
takeaway: Cross-train endurance events alongside Hyrox to build a deeper aerobic base.

name: Vivian Tafuto
who: Full-time actuary and Elite 15 podium regular; with Lauren Weeks holds the women's doubles world record (52:59).
why: Proof a full-time job and elite Hyrox racing aren't mutually exclusive, plus a doubles world record.
takeaway: Fit elite-level training around a full-time career — a demanding job doesn't rule out podiums.

name: Sinéad Bent
who: UK physiotherapist and Elite 15 athlete who went from newcomer to elite level in a single year.
why: A fast-rising British racer with a genuinely engaged following and brand deals (Gymshark, Garmin) to match.
takeaway: Use knowledge of your own body's mechanics to fast-track from newcomer to elite.

name: Meg Martin
who: Australian Elite 15 doubles racer; with Calypso Sheridan holds the women's doubles world record (53:21) and placed 5th at the 2026 World Championships.
why: A record-setting doubles specialist whose M3GA brand and run clubs reach well beyond the racecourse.
takeaway: Commit to one fixed doubles partner and drill pacing together toward a target time.

name: Lucy Procter
who: 22-year-old Red Bull/Puma-backed Elite 15 racer and 2024 Hyrox U24 world champion.
why: One of the youngest names in the Elite 15 and already climbing the senior world rankings.
takeaway: Start racing age-group divisions young to build competitive experience before moving up to senior fields.

name: Danél Louw
who: South African Hyrox Pro-division champion (Johannesburg, Cape Town) chasing an Elite 15 World Championship podium.
why: The sport's clearest breakout story out of South Africa, now backed by a growing brand roster.
takeaway: Build your Hyrox résumé at home first before targeting an Elite 15 world podium.

name: Calypso Sheridan
who: Australian Elite 15 singles and doubles racer; with Meg Martin set the women's doubles world record (53:21) and finished top 5 at the 2026 Worlds.
why: A double threat racing both the singles Elite 15 and record-setting doubles.
takeaway: Race both the singles Elite 15 field and doubles events in the same season.

name: Emilie Dahmen
who: Dutch Elite 15 singles racer, ranked inside the current world top 10 heading into the 2026 World Championships.
why: The Netherlands' top Hyrox export, holding a steady top-10 world ranking.
takeaway: Aim for a steady top-10 world ranking through consistency rather than chasing one peak race.

name: Seka Arning
who: German Elite 15 singles racer for the 2026 World Championships in Stockholm.
why: One of three Germans in the current Elite 15 women's field, evidence of the country's rising depth.
takeaway: Train inside a strong national group — surrounding yourself with other elite racers raises your own level.

name: Alyssa McElheny
who: American Elite 15 singles racer for the 2026 World Championships in Stockholm.
why: Part of the deep US contingent pushing the pace at every major.
takeaway: Train inside a deep national field — pushing against strong training partners raises your pace.

name: Jess Pettrow
who: Australian Elite 15 singles racer, part of the country's deep women's contingent alongside Wietrzyk and Sheridan.
why: A steady major-race performer with room to climb the Elite 15 ranks.
takeaway: Keep showing up at major races steadily — consistent starts build the ranking climb over time.

name: Morgan Schulz
who: American Elite 15 singles racer for the 2026 World Championships in Stockholm.
why: Another deep-bench US racer keeping the field honest week to week.
takeaway: Compete inside a deep bench of racers — consistent starts keep you sharp for bigger meets.

name: Gabrielle Nikora-Baker
who: New Zealand's Elite 15 singles racer for the 2026 World Championships.
why: The only Kiwi in the current Elite 15 women's field.
takeaway: Represent your country's scene even without local peers at your level — go race the world field anyway.

name: Lena Putters
who: Belgian Elite 15 singles racer for the 2026 World Championships.
why: Belgium's flag-bearer in the world's toughest field.
takeaway: Race for your country's flag even in the toughest field, and help build the depth behind you.

name: Stefanie Oswald
who: German Elite 15 singles racer for the 2026 World Championships in Stockholm.
why: The third German name in the current Elite 15 — depth that's reshaping the leaderboard.
takeaway: Contribute to your national scene's depth — one more elite name raises the whole field around it.
